Solution:
Let G be an undirected graph. Demonstrate that every cut in G can be expressed
as the disjoint union of minimal cuts.
Definition 1 (Cut and Cut-set). Let G = (V, E) be an undirected graph. For a partition of
the vertex set V = S ⊔T with S, T ̸= ∅, the cut-set (or simply cut) associated with this
partition is
δ(S) = E(S, T) = {e ∈E : e has one endpoint in S and one in T}.
Definition 2 (Minimal Cut / Bond). A cut C = δ(S) is called minimal (or a bond) if
no proper subset of C is a cut-set for any partition of V . Equivalently, C is minimal if
it is a minimal non-empty set of edges whose removal increases the number of connected
components of G.
Theorem 1. Every cut in an undirected graph G can be expressed as a disjoint union of
minimal cuts (bonds).
Proof. Let G = (V, E) be an undirected graph, and let C = δ(S) be a cut corresponding to
the partition V = S ⊔T.
Step 1: Decompose into components.
Consider the subgraphs induced by S and T:
• Let S1, S2, . . . , Sp be the vertex sets of the connected components of G[S], the subgraph
induced by S.
• Let T1, T2, . . . , Tq be the vertex sets of the connected components of G[T], the subgraph
induced by T.
Step 2: Partition the cut by component pairs.
For each pair (i, j) with 1 ≤i ≤p and 1 ≤j ≤q, define
Cij = {e ∈C : e connects a vertex in Si to a vertex in Tj}.
Since each edge in C connects some component Si to some component Tj, and these
connections are unique, we have

Step 3: Show each non-empty Cij is a minimal cut.
Let Cij ̸= ∅for some pair (i, j). We prove that Cij = δ(Si) is a bond.
Claim: Cij is a cut-set.
Consider the partition V = Si ⊔(V \ Si). Any edge in E(Si, V \ Si) either:
• connects Si to some Si′ ̸= Si (impossible since Si is a connected component of G[S]
and all such edges would be in S), or

Cij, plus possibly edges from other Si′ to Tj.
More precisely, Cij ⊆δ(Tj). But we claim that Cij = δ(Tj) ∩δ(Si) when both sets are
considered within the context of the original cut.
Claim: Cij is minimal.
Suppose C′ ⊂Cij is a proper subset that is also a cut-set. Then removing C′ from
G increases the number of connected components. But Si is connected in G (since it’s a
component of G[S]), and Tj is connected in G (since it’s a component of G[T]). The only
edges connecting Si and Tj are those in Cij.
If we remove only C′ ⊂Cij, there still exist edges in Cij \ C′ connecting Si to Tj.
Therefore, there exists a path from any vertex in Si to any vertex in Tj using edges not in
C′. This means C′ does not separate Si from Tj, and since all other components were already
determined by the original partition, C′ cannot be a cut-set—a contradiction.
Therefore, each non-empty Cij is a minimal cut, and we have expressed C as a disjoint
union of minimal cuts.
Remark. This result is fundamental in the theory of graphic matroids and the bond space of
a graph. The minimal cuts (bonds) can be viewed as the fundamental elements that generate
all cuts through symmetric differences.

fields.explanation: The original C4 edges01,12,23,03 and bipartition{0,2}|{1,3} are unchanged. Induced graphs are empty, so their components are singletons. Block{01} differs from cut{01,03}, and deleting block{01} leaves the graph connected. The selected theorem certifies the source-qualified primary counterexample. Historical auxiliary sweeps are not silently promoted to universal statements. The original sufficient repair assumes both induced sides G[S] and G[V\S] are connected and nonempty. Then each side has only one component, so its component-pair crossing block is the entire cut. Deleting every crossing edge disconnects the sides, while retaining even one crossing edge connects the two internally connected sides. The cut is therefore inclusion-minimal; the unrestricted disconnected-side inference does not follow.
fields.flaw: Step 3 of the proof: every non-empty block C_ij (the set of edges joining a connected component S_i of G[S] to a connected component T_j of G[T]) equals delta(S_i) and is a minimal cut (bond). A 4-vertex graph shows a non-empty C_ij that is not even a cut-set (its removal does not increase the number of connected components), and also C_ij != delta(S_i).

fields.witness: Headline witness (4 vertices, G connected): G = C_4, the 4-cycle on V = {0,1,2,3} with E = {0-1, 1-2, 2-3, 0-3}. Take the bipartition S = {0,2}, T = {1,3}. Both induced subgraphs are edgeless, so G[S] has components S_1 = {0}, S_2 = {2} and G[T] has components T_1 = {1}, T_2 = {3}. The block C_11 = edges from S_1 to T_1 = {0-1} is non-empty. Recomputed quantities: delta(S_1) = delta({0}) = {0-1, 0-3}, so the proof says C_11 = delta(S_1) but here C_11 = {0-1} != {0-1, 0-3} = delta(S_1), with delta(S_1) \ C_11 = {0-3} (an edge from S_1 to the OTHER T-component). Moreover #components(G) = 1 and #components(G - C_11) = 1 (the path 1-2-3-0 remains connected), so "deleting C_11 strictly increases the number of components" is false: 1 > 1 is FALSE. C_11 is therefore not even a cut-set, let alone a minimal cut (bond). The same happens for all four blocks by symmetry. Smaller (3-vertex) witness for the equality half only: the path G = {0-1, 0-2} with S = {0}, T = {1,2}: S_1 = {0}, T_1 = {1}, T_2 = {2}, C_11 = {0-1} != {0-1, 0-2} = delta(S_1) (here C_11 does happen to be a bond, so it refutes only the "C_ij = delta(S_i)" half; the 4-cycle refutes both halves).
